title: Falls in older people: getting help and rebuilding confidence
intro: A fall is not an unavoidable part of growing older, and it should not be dismissed as clumsiness. Vision, balance, muscle strength, medicines, illness and the home environment can contribute together. Assessment after a fall can uncover treatable problems and reduce future risk. The aim is to support independence and safe movement, not simply restrict activity.

sections.heading: Check for injury before trying to get up
paragraphs: Stay calm and check pain, breathing and how you feel. Do not force yourself to stand or allow someone to pull you up if a fracture or head, neck, back or hip injury is possible. Call 112 for suspected serious injury, inability to get up, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or new stroke-like symptoms. If waiting on the floor, use a reachable phone or alarm, call out and keep warm. After a head injury, tell the assessing service about blood thinners even if you initially feel well; problems may not be immediately obvious.

sections.heading: Tell a clinician what happened, including near misses
paragraphs: Arrange review after a fall, repeated near falls or new balance concerns. Describe the location, footwear, lighting, activity, dizziness, possible blackout and whether anyone witnessed the event. Bring all medicines, including sleeping tablets and non-prescription products. Assessment may cover walking, balance, strength, blood pressure when changing position, vision, feet, heart symptoms and home hazards. A fall associated with fainting is not necessarily a simple trip. Do not stop medicines yourself; ask for a review of benefits, unwanted effects and safer alternatives where appropriate.

sections.heading: Reduce hazards with practical changes
paragraphs: Check loose rugs, cables, clutter, slippery floors, steps and the route to the toilet at night. Improve lighting, keep commonly used items within reach and choose well-fitting footwear with secure support and grip. Ask for help fitting grab rails or other adaptations safely; a towel rail is not automatically a safe handhold. A walking aid should fit you and be used correctly, rather than borrowed without assessment. An occupational therapist or local support service may help prioritize affordable changes, while preserving the person’s preferences and usual activities.

sections.heading: Build strength and address other health risks
paragraphs: An individual exercise programme emphasizing balance and muscle strength can help reduce falls. A physiotherapist can choose a safe starting point, especially after injury, with frailty or when using a walking aid. Gradually increasing activity is often better than avoiding movement because of fear. Arrange appropriate eye care, discuss dizziness and foot problems, and maintain suitable food and fluid intake within any medical restrictions. Ask about bone health and osteoporosis risk, because fracture prevention also matters. Supplements are not a substitute for assessment and are not automatically needed by everyone.

sections.heading: Make a plan for confidence, support and another fall
paragraphs: Keep a phone or personal alarm accessible and discuss a realistic way to obtain help. Ask a trained professional to teach a safe floor-rise strategy suited to your abilities rather than practicing alone after an injury. Tell someone if fear of falling has stopped you leaving home, washing or doing daily tasks; rehabilitation and psychological support can help. Review the plan after any new fall or change in health. Caregivers should avoid lifting someone manually or restricting them without considering safer support, consent and independence.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a nighttime trip
examples.text: Maria trips on a loose rug on the way to the bathroom. After injury assessment, she and an adviser improve lighting, clear the route and discuss suitable footwear. They also review dizziness instead of assuming the rug was the only cause.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: confidence after a fall
examples.text: Petar stops walking outside because he fears another fall. A physiotherapist develops supported strength and balance work, and his family helps arrange short outings and an accessible phone. Progress is gradual; nobody promises that one aid removes every risk.

questions: Could illness, a blackout or medicines have contributed, and what assessment is needed?
